So, he turned back into the domain. The street was quiet in the perpetual night of the domain — the generators finished, the gate opened, the survivors gone and the trial technically over. Whatever the Fog did with itself in the spaces between, it did it silently. Usually, he would have been spirited away by now and dumped into the next area. Being able to freely wander an empty domain after a trial felt wrong somehow. Danny wandered the empty street, each step squelching softly through mud and silt, until the familiar bulk of the preschool rose into view again. The surrounding area had taken the full force of the exit — the yard churned, the fence buckled in places where lockers had introduced themselves to it, plaster and debris scattered across the asphalt and pooling in the gutters. The building itself looked scoured. Pressure washed empty, and left to drip dry across the lawn. It wasn't permanent. He knew that. The next time a trial was called here the Fog would reset the whole domain — pull the debris back, drain the water, restore the geometry to its original footprint and set the crows back on their perches as if none of it had happened. That was just how it worked. The Fog didn't hold onto damage. He wasn't sure yet if that was a comfort. The absence was what hit hardest. The rot, the weight, the invisible pulse of malice that had choked the walls for hours — it was gone. No pressure at the edges of his awareness. No sense of being observed. Just the domain, and the debris, and the distant sound of water still draining somewhere in the building's bones. She had spent Herself on this. Used everything She had and come away empty-handed, and now She was simply — gone. Recovering somewhere in the architecture of Her own realm, presumably. Licking Her wounds. He limped through the yard, sidestepping a half-sunk filing cabinet in the mud. His ribs reminded him of their existence with every step — the bandage was doing its work, but it’s not like it could perform miracles. The debris was everywhere — lockers wedged against the fence at improbable angles, plaster smeared in wide arcs across the rusted swing set, a filing cabinet embedded nose-first in a flower bed that had never had flowers in it. The playground wore the evidence of the night — it, too, seemed to be a victim of the Entity’s little game. He picked his way through it slowly, not in any particular hurry, the silence of it settling around him one step at a time. He reached the side entrance and kicked a chunk of door frame out of the path. Then another. The broken killer wall gaped open above the debris line, the edges of it ragged and splintered outward, wood shrapnel scattered across the grass in an impressive radius. Danny toed aside a chunk of molding, eyeing the wreckage with something almost like respect. The damage was impressive. Not just the final breach — the whole face of the wall told the story of what had happened in the alcove, the wood bearing the accumulated record of every kick in a pattern of stress fractures that radiated outward from the centre. Whatever the killer walls were made of, it wasn't meant to come apart like this. It wasn't meant to come apart at all. That was the point of them. Danny ran his fingers along the splintered edge, reading the force of it in the grain. “...Gold star, brawler,” he muttered with a slight chuckle. The stocky little brat had been underwater, out of air, running on something past exhaustion and past rage and past whatever came after rage — and he'd broken the damned wall anyway. Danny pulled his hand back from the wood. He turned the thought over once, quiet and private in the empty domain. If the man ever had the inclination to swap sides — the desire, the circumstance, whatever it would take — he would be a genuinely terrifying thing to face in a trial. The Fog would probably be delighted. The survivors considerably less so. Danny leaned against the doorframe and let it hold some of his weight. The ribs made themselves known about that, a low persistent complaint that the bandage was managing but not solving. He'd be dealing with them for a while. He was used to discomfort, generally speaking — the Fog had a particular relationship with pain that kept things functional without making them comfortable — but this was a specific, personal kind of ache that felt different from the usual wear of a trial. More earned, maybe. Definitely deserved, at the very least. He leaned against the splintered doorway, letting his shoulder slump against the frame. The hallway inside was back to normal. Tight. Short. Still cracked and peeling in that aesthetic decay way, but no longer a shapeshifting maze full of pressure and current. No longer a black chasm of currents and chaos. No screaming. He hadn't expected to feel anything in particular about that. Still, there was a strange sort of relief; the specific comfort of a space that was just a space again and wasn't trying to kill anyone. After the hallways stretching and the currents and the pipes and the ceiling arriving in increments, ordinary was something he could handle. Ordinary gave him the time to stop, rest a bit, and let the silence of it settle around him, trying not to think too hard about what came next. He pushed off from the doorframe. There was likely somewhere in the building that was probably drier than the rest of it. If not, there were other small, busted buildings in the area that would suffice. He could sleep
